context: Each move climbs 1 or 2 stairs, and dp[i] is the number of ways to reach stair i. Brute-force search applies the recurrence dp[i] = dp[i − 1] + dp[i − 2] recursively until it reaches a base case, dp[1] = 1 or dp[2] = 2.
description: Computing dp[9] requires dp[8] and dp[7]. Computing dp[8] in turn requires dp[7] and dp[6]. The two occurrences of dp[7] in the brute-force tree do not share a computation. Each call expands and solves the subproblem for itself.

The figure shows only the first four levels, with 15 state nodes in all. The 16 ellipses at the bottom indicate that recursion continues to the base cases dp[1] or dp[2]. Counts in the table, such as the 4 occurrences of dp[5], cover only the four levels shown, rather than the entire recursion.

The tables first list the four levels shown, then summarize them by state. The breakdown table gives the left and right subproblems from the recurrence. Ellipses stand in for the children of all nodes on level 4. In particular, dp[4] and dp[3] appear only on level 4. The subproblems in those two rows follow from the recurrence and are not drawn individually.

frames.explanation: The caption at the bottom connects overlapping subproblems to exponential running time: brute-force recursion solves the same states repeatedly, giving it time complexity O(2^n).
frames.title: Overlapping subproblems in a brute-force stair-climbing search

summary: When brute-force recursion breaks down dp[9] from the top down, identical subproblems share no results. Different branches expand and solve them repeatedly.
